The Brazilian stardrum Stellifer naso exhibits several key life-history traits that have been characterized from field-collected specimens in coastal waters of the western South Atlantic. Examination of adult individuals indicates that this sciaenid species attains a maximum recorded total body length of 20.0 centimeters [Li = 20.0 centimeters], a size that appears to represent the upper limit of somatic growth for the species within its natural range. The ultimate wet body mass corresponding to this asymptotic length has been estimated at 63.5 grams [Wwi = 63.5 grams] based on length-weight regressions derived from local population samples. This moderate adult size is consistent with the general body plan observed among several small-to-medium-bodied Stellifer species that occupy shallow estuarine and nearshore environments along the Brazilian coastline, where prey availability and thermal regimes likely constrain maximum attainable dimensions.

Sexual maturation in female Brazilian stardrum is initiated at a relatively modest body size compared to the ultimate adult length. Specifically, the total length at which females first become capable of reproducing has been determined to be 10.7 centimeters [Lp = 10.7 centimeters]. At this length, the corresponding wet weight at puberty for females is approximately 9.7 grams [Wwp = approximately 9.7 grams], reflecting the energetic investment required to support gonadal development and the onset of vitellogenesis. This size at maturity, representing just over half of the ultimate length, is typical of many iteroparous sciaenids that experience size-selective predation pressure in coastal nurseries, where earlier maturation may enhance the probability of contributing to the next generation before encountering age-specific mortality risks.

Reproductive output in Stellifer naso has been studied under controlled conditions that closely mimic the thermal environment of its natural habitat, with experimental populations maintained at a stable water temperature of 23.9 °C [T = 23.9 °C]. Females under these conditions are capable of producing approximately 25,171 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 25,171 eggs per year]. This high annual fecundity reflects the species' strategy of producing numerous pelagic eggs, a common trait among marine teleosts that broadcast their propagules into the water column, where early life stages face exceptionally high mortality rates from predation and environmental variability. The ability to sustain such elevated reproductive output over sequential spawning events within a single year highlights the energetic efficiency of this species' physiological machinery, even when compared to other sciaenids of similar body size inhabiting the same estuarine systems.

The early life stages of the Brazilian stardrum begin with the release of small, pelagic eggs that undergo embryonic development externally. Upon fertilization, each yolk-laden egg has an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.00053 grams [Wwb = 0.00053 grams], a value derived from the standard geometric relationship for a spherical egg with a diameter of approximately one millimeter. This minute initial mass is typical of sciaenids that produce numerous small offspring as a means of dispersing propagules over broad spatial scales, thereby exploiting patchily distributed planktonic food resources. Following eclosion, the prolarvae remain entirely dependent on their endogenous yolk reserves for several days until the mouth opens and the trophic switch to exogenous feeding occurs, a critical transition in the species' early ontogeny that is marked by the onset of active prey capture and the commencement of rapid somatic growth. The timing of this developmental milestone is tightly linked to water temperature, with warmer conditions accelerating the depletion of the yolk sac and hastening the transition to a free-swimming, exogenously feeding larva.

Longevity data for Stellifer naso, inferred from captive-maintained cohorts held at a stable thermal regime of 23.9 °C [T = 23.9 °C], indicate that individuals can attain a maximum lifespan of approximately 11 years [am = approximately 11 years]. This relatively extended lifespan is noteworthy for a small-bodied sciaenid and suggests that adults experience comparatively low natural mortality rates once they have recruited to the benthic juvenile stage in estuarine refuges. The combination of moderate body size, early maturation at 10.7 centimeters [Lp = 10.7 centimeters] total length, high annual fecundity, and a multi-year reproductive window positions this species as a classic K-selected strategist among the coastal fishes of eastern South America. In comparison to congeneric species such as Stellifer stellifer and Stellifer brasiliensis, the Brazilian stardrum exhibits a longer maximum lifespan and a slightly larger asymptotic body size, traits that may confer a competitive advantage in stable, low-disturbance estuarine environments where the ability to defer reproduction and invest in somatic growth yields higher lifetime fitness returns.
